specPoints.text: understand how germinating seeds utilise food reserves until the seedling can carry out photosynthesis

primer.text: A seed is a survival kit: a baby plant, two starter leaves and a packed food store, all sealed in a coat. This note follows germination, the moment water switches the kit on — enzymes dismantle the stored starch into glucose, respiration burns it, and growth runs on that energy until the first leaves can photosynthesise.

lessons.title: Living Off the Packed Lunch
lessons.opening: A seed carries four survival parts — a baby shoot, a baby root, seed leaves called cotyledons and a starchy food store; at germination enzymes slice that reserve into maltose and then glucose, and respiration pays for the growing shoot and root until real leaves take over.
keyPoints: A seed packages four parts: a baby shoot, a baby root, seed leaves called cotyledons and a starchy food store.
During germination the embryo grows using the food reserves in the store.
Enzymes break the stored starch into maltose and then glucose.
Glucose then fuels respiration, releasing energy that pays for shoot and root growth.
Photosynthesis takes over once the seedling's larger leaves emerge.

low.restatement: The seed eats its own packed lunch: starch is digested to glucose and burned for growth energy until leaves appear.
low.analogy: A hiker living off trail rations until the first farm stop, then grows their own food.
low.examPointer: Name the chain — starch, maltose, glucose — and end with photosynthesis taking over.

medium.restatement: Nothing photosynthetic works in a buried seed, so the entire energy budget comes from stored starch; enzymes keep the sugar flowing, and respiration pays for cell division in the shoot and root until leaves expand enough to fund the plant themselves.
medium.analogy: A relay race: the food store hands energy to respiration, which hands the seedling to sunlight.
medium.examPointer: Say why the store is essential — the embryo cannot photosynthesise before leaves exist.

check.stem: Which parts does a seed contain?

options.text: A baby shoot, a baby root, cotyledons and a food store
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Flower petals and sepals
options.explanation: Petals belong to flowers, not seeds.

options.text: Pollen grains and ovules
options.explanation: Those are flower gamete structures, not seed contents.

options.text: Fruit flesh and hooks
options.explanation: Fruit surrounds seeds; it is not inside them.

check.stem: What do enzymes do to the stored starch during germination?

options.text: Break it down into maltose and then glucose
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Turn it straight into oxygen
options.explanation: Starch digestion never makes oxygen.

options.text: Convert it into new seeds
options.explanation: Stored starch fuels growth, not seed production.

options.text: Burn it without sugar steps
options.explanation: Digestion passes through maltose before glucose.

check.stem: Why does the germinating seed respire the glucose it releases?

options.text: To release energy for growth of the embryo shoot and root
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: To store the glucose as more starch
options.explanation: The store is being spent, not refilled.

options.text: To make chlorophyll before leaves grow
options.explanation: Chlorophyll belongs to the leaves that follow.

options.text: To attract pollinators to the seedling
options.explanation: Seedlings are underground; no pollinators visit.

check.stem: When can the new plant stop relying on its food store?

options.text: Once larger leaves emerge and photosynthesis begins
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: As soon as water enters the seed
options.explanation: Water starts germination; the store still feeds the plant.

options.text: Once the roots reach soil
options.explanation: Roots absorb water, not food for growth.

options.text: Only after flowers open
options.explanation: Flowering comes long after the store is spent.

check.stem: A seedling is grown in complete darkness until its leaves open. Why does it survive the dark phase?

options.text: Its food store supplies respiration with glucose until light lets photosynthesis start
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Darkness speeds up starch storage
options.explanation: Nothing stores new starch in the dark.

options.text: The seed photosynthesises underground
options.explanation: No light means no photosynthesis.

options.text: Respiration is switched off until light
options.explanation: Respiration must run to release energy for growth.

check.stem: Name the seed leaves found inside a seed.
check.modelAnswer: The seed leaves found inside a seed are known as cotyledons.

check.stem: State the two sugars produced as stored starch is digested in germination.
check.modelAnswer: Stored starch is broken into maltose and then glucose.

check.stem: Explain why the food store is vital to the seedling before its leaves expand.
check.modelAnswer: Without expanded leaves the seedling cannot photosynthesise, so respiration must burn glucose from the food store to release the energy growth requires.

check.stem: A weighing experiment shows a germinating seed losing dry mass. Explain the loss using the seed's energy budget.
check.modelAnswer: Respiration converts the store's glucose into energy and releases carbon dioxide, so stored dry mass leaves the seed as gas while the seedling grows.

glossary.definition: A seed leaf; the part of the seed that often stores food for germination.
The starch-rich reserve inside a seed that fuels growth until photosynthesis starts.
The beginning of seed growth, when the embryo uses the food reserves to grow.

figures.alt: Diagram showing seed germination stages: embryo, seed coat, cotyledon, foliage leaves, roots, and shoots, illustrating plant growth progression.
